history.alt_text: An imbalanced stack of blank shipping boxes leaning heavily to one side on a steel warehouse floor.
history.caption: When supply chain models confuse promotional pull-forward with true demand, the resulting inventory imbalance carries a heavy margin cost.
history.title: Borrowed Demand Inventory Imbalance

style_when: the story is a product, a device, a price or a market for a thing the reader could buy — an appliance, a panel, a router, a robot arm
prompt: An imbalanced, towering stack of blank cardboard shipping boxes leaning precariously to the left, standing on a brushed steel warehouse loading bay floor. 100mm studio product photograph, extreme asymmetry with heavy editorial negative space on the right. Softbox key light from the left casting a long, dark contact shadow across the textured steel surface. Slate grey, bone white, and weathered orange palette. Shallow depth of field, fine film grain, catalogue clarity, no people, no text.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random letters, numbers, UI, watermarks, people, faces
rationale: The story revolves around the misinterpretation of physical inventory demand (retail goods/boxes) and the economic cost of that misinterpretation. A studio object approach allows for a highly controlled, dramatic representation of an imbalanced inventory stack, symbolizing the 'borrowed' demand and the precarious nature of the forecast.
cue: A promo lends units from nearby weeks
subject: An imbalanced, towering stack of blank cardboard shipping boxes leaning precariously
core_thesis: Promotional demand spikes borrow sales from adjacent periods while standing price cuts erode margin, yet standard forecasting models dangerously treat both as true underlying demand, leading to costly inventory and factory overreactions.
core_conflict: Phantom demand signals vs. true baseline consumption, and the margin cost of misinterpreting promotional pull-forward as organic growth.
composition: extreme asymmetry with heavy editorial negative space
